title: Conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, on input a finite one-relator group presentation \(G=\langle x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k} | r=1\rangle\) and two words u,v, decides whether some word w satisfies \(w^{- 1}uw=v\) in G?
definitions: The input consists of an integer \(k\ge 1\) and three explicitly written finite words r,u,v over the letters \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}\) and their formal inverses. The group is the quotient of the free group \(F(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k})\) by the normal subgroup generated by r. The relator may be empty, in which case G is free. Equality in the displayed equation is equality in this quotient, rather than literal equality of strings. A conjugating word w may have any finite length. The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine that must halt with the correct yes/no answer for every valid input; the presentation is part of the input. No polynomial-time or other specified resource bound is imposed. This is the uniform decision formulation; a separate algorithm for each fixed group, without an effective way to obtain it from a presentation, is not by itself sufficient.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such presentations and pairs of words, or prove that this input language is undecidable. A one-relator group with an undecidable fixed-group conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer. A result only for torsion groups, a decision procedure for word equality, or undecidability of a different equation or membership problem does not settle this question.
why: A central decision problem at the boundary between decidable symbolic equality and existential reasoning in finitely presented algebraic structures.

importance.reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.

progress.text: Magnus establishes decidability of the word problem for one-relator groups. This does not decide conjugacy.
Newman proves decidability of the conjugacy problem for all one-relator groups with torsion.
Minasyan–Zalesskii prove hereditary conjugacy separability for one-relator groups with torsion.
Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s comprehensive survey records the general conjugacy problem as open and describes why the word-problem induction does not automatically extend.
Gray–Levine obtain undecidability results for related Diophantine problems, including subgroup-constrained equations; these do not settle unrestricted conjugacy.
Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of unrestricted Diophantine problems in one-relator groups while explicitly retaining conjugacy as an open question.
Gray–Reilly obtain two-generator inverse-monoid word and group prefix-membership undecidability, which are distinct from this group conjugacy question.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general conjugacy problem remains open in the checked primary literature. This card fixes the uniform presentation-input formulation. The 2026 undecidability results cited concern different equation, membership or inverse-monoid problems.

context_blocks.text: A finite presentation describes a group through generators and identities. Here there is just one defining identity, but it can be reused inside arbitrarily long products. The conjugacy question asks whether two elements become equal after a change of reference element: u and v are equivalent when \(v=w^{- 1}uw\). It is one of Dehn’s classical decision problems. The 2025 survey explicitly identifies the general one-relator conjugacy problem as unresolved.

Conjugacy is already different from equality in a free group. The words ab and ba are conjugate, since \(a^{- 1}(ab)a=ba\), although they represent different free-group elements. At the opposite extreme, the identity element is conjugate only to itself. Consequently, a conjugacy algorithm also decides whether an input word represents the identity, by setting v to the empty word. The reverse implication is the difficult part.

Magnus’s 1932 theorem supplies a uniform algorithm for word equality in one-relator groups. Its inductive approach, clarified through the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, decomposes presentations into simpler group constructions. The corresponding transfer of conjugacy algorithms is much more delicate: the survey gives examples of HNN extensions and amalgams with undecidable conjugacy even though the relevant word problems are decidable. These examples explain a barrier to extending the proof; they are not one-relator counterexamples.

The known word algorithm does at least give a positive semidecision procedure for the present question. Enumerate all finite words w and test whether \(w^{- 1}\)uwv\(^{- 1}\) represents the identity. If u and v are conjugate, a witness eventually appears. If they are not, this search continues forever. A complete decision procedure must also provide a way to terminate on every negative input.

Equivalently, one could give a computable uniform bound on the length of a shortest necessary conjugator as a function of the input length. Such a bound permits a finite search. Conversely, a decision procedure permits computing a bound: enumerate the finitely many inputs of bounded encoding length, identify the positive ones, and search for one witness for each. This observation concerns computability, without claiming that a useful or small bound follows.

The torsion case has been solved for decades. Newman’s 1968 thesis proves decidability of conjugacy for one-relator groups with torsion, including an extended conjugacy problem relative to specified subgroups. Standard presentations for this class have relator \(R^{m}\) with \(m\ge 2\) and R not a proper power. The spelling theorem controls the possible cancellations strongly enough to support effective arguments. A solution for this class leaves the general torsion-free case to address.

A later structural theorem gives another source of negative certificates in the torsion case. Minasyan–Zalesskii prove that one-relator groups with torsion are hereditarily conjugacy separable: nonconjugate elements in every finite-index subgroup remain nonconjugate in some finite quotient of that subgroup. In particular, for the original group, a finite quotient can witness a negative conjugacy answer.

To see the algorithmic significance, enumerate finite multiplication tables and assignments of the presentation’s generators that satisfy its relator. Each assignment defines a homomorphism to a finite group, where conjugacy can be checked exhaustively. In a conjugacy-separable group, this search eventually finds a separating image for every nonconjugate pair. Run it alongside the search for a conjugator. The argument requires the separation property; finite images alone are not a general-purpose certificate system.

Recent developments illustrate why the exact decision problem matters. Gray–Levine prove undecidability of Diophantine problems in several classes close to one-relator groups, and also obtain undecidability with a fixed subgroup constraint in a one-relator group. General systems of equations, or restrictions on where variables may range, are more expressive than the single unrestricted conjugacy equation on this card. Undecidability for those tasks does not imply undecidability here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 3, 2026 preprint goes further: it proves that the unrestricted Diophantine problem is undecidable in certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its introduction still explicitly identifies general one-relator conjugacy as open. Undecidability for arbitrary systems of equations therefore cannot be substituted for undecidability of the special single conjugacy equation.

Gray–Reilly’s August 2026 preprint constructs two-generator one-relator inverse monoids with undecidable word problem. It also constructs a two-generator one-relator group with an undecidable prefix membership problem. Inverse monoids are a different algebraic structure, while prefix membership asks about a particular submonoid of the group. Neither result contradicts Magnus’s word algorithm or supplies a conjugacy counterexample.

The significance is a sharp computability boundary inside an extremely economical symbolic formalism. One defining group relation is sufficient to create complicated infinite behavior, yet ordinary equality remains decidable. Settling conjugacy would determine whether this additional existential search can always be controlled. A very slow total algorithm would answer the card; an efficient algorithm for a broad but restricted subclass would be progress without completing it.

category_assignment.reason: The problem decides conjugacy of elements of finitely presented one-relator groups.

sentences: Conjugacy asks whether two group elements differ by a transformation of the form \(w^{- 1}uw\).
The reviewed question seeks one algorithm deciding this for every finitely presented group with a single defining relation.
Equality of words is decidable in these groups, but searching possible conjugators only semidecides positive answers.
An algorithm would settle a classical decision problem for a remarkably concise family of infinite algebraic structures.
The saved review explains that decomposition methods preserving word-problem decidability do not automatically preserve decidable conjugacy.
